newsitem.title: USA: Democrats press U.S. pension plan reforms. [CORRECTED 23:16 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Democrats press U.S. pension plan reforms. [CORRECTED 23:16 GMT]

text.p: Senate Democrats said Thursday (corrects from Wednesday) they will push next year for pension law reforms making it easier for small firms to offer pensions and allow employees to carry their pensions from job to job.

Sens. Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts and Jeff Bingaman of New Mexico told reporters a key element would be new tax incentives for companies to offer pensions and a new congressionally chartered private clearinghouse to run the funds for small businesses.
"We need to reform the 'Alice in Wonderland' effect of the tax laws that grant the greatest subsidy to the wealthiest employees," Kennedy said at a news conference.

The companies could enroll their employees without having to jump over the complicated legal hurdles now required to set up a 401(k) pension plan. The employees would remain in the plan even if they switched jobs.

During his presidential campaign, President Clinton announced the Treasury Department would help workers roll over retirement savings into a new employer's plan by lifting legal barriers to the shift of funds.
However the plan outlined by the senators would go further and would provide additional tax subsidies to encourage companies to contribute for employees.

The amount of the tax incentive for employers and for employees has not yet been set and the size of the revenue loss to the government has not been calculated. New tax breaks are not permitted to add to the federal budget deficit and must be offset in some way.

Over 50 million workers have no private pension plan and most work in small companies with fewer than 25 employees and earn less than $30,000 a year. Washington provides $66 billion in tax subsidies for pension coverage, most of which benefits higher income persons who have the greatest participation in private pensions plans.

Kennedy also said Congress should do more to diversify investments made by all retirement plans. "Employees should not be forced to invest their own retirement contributions in the employer's stock against their wishes," he added.

The pension legislation is still being written and is expected to be introduced in January when Congress returns. It may move on two tracks -- a Democratic plan included in the party's "Families First" agenda, and a bipartisan plan offered by Bingaman and Republicans. Bingaman said he hopes to work with Sen. James Jeffords, now incoming chairman of the Labour Committee, as he did last year on the proposed Pension "Pro-Save" plan which set up the Pension Portability Clearinghouse.

Other elements of the Democratic plan could include more protection for holders of 401(k) retirement accounts managed by employers, additional steps to help women gain pension coverage and changes in Individual Retirement Accounts.
